title: Pinkeye in sheep: recognising and treating it
subtitle: Identifying infectious keratoconjunctivitis and acting before it causes blindness.
excerpt: Pinkeye in sheep spreads fast through a flock during summer, particularly in dusty conditions, fly pressure, and bright sunlight. Caught early it responds well to a single course of oxytetracycline eye ointment or a long-acting injectable. Left more than a few days it can cause corneal scarring and permanent vision loss. Spot it by the weeping eye, the half-closed squint, and the washed-out cloudy cornea.
sourceNotes: AHDB Beef and Lamb, Sheep health and disease: infectious keratoconjunctivitis (2022). DEFRA Code of Recommendations for the Welfare of Sheep (2018). Moredun Research Institute, Eye problems in sheep (2021). NADIS (National Animal Disease Information Service), pinkeye factsheet (2023).

glossaryTerms.definition: Infectious keratoconjunctivitis in sheep, caused by Mycoplasma conjunctivae and associated bacteria. It produces weeping, squinting, and clouding of the cornea, and spreads rapidly through close contact.

The clear protective outer surface of the eye. In pinkeye, the cornea becomes cloudy or blue-white as the infection penetrates the outer layers. Severe scarring of the cornea causes permanent vision impairment.

content.text: Pinkeye

in sheep is infectious keratoconjunctivitis caused by Mycoplasma and associated bacteria. It spreads between sheep at close contact, particularly in hot dry summers when dust, bright light, and face flies create ideal conditions. A single affected sheep in a group can infect several others within a week.
What to look for
Watery eye or tear staining down the face below the affected eye.
Half-closed squint: the sheep holds the eye partially or fully closed in response to light sensitivity.
Clouding of the
cornea

: the normally clear outer eye surface goes grey-white or bluish. This is the sign that infection has progressed into the corneal tissue and the prognosis for full recovery depends on how soon treatment starts.
In advanced cases, a white ulcer may be visible on the corneal surface. At this stage the risk of permanent vision loss is high.

Separate any sheep showing eye signs from the main group as soon as you spot them. Separating affected animals reduces transmission and allows you to monitor treatment response without losing track of which animals have been treated.
Treatment

Oxytetracycline is the standard first-line treatment. It is available as an eye ointment (applied directly to the eye) or a long-acting injectable, administered subcutaneously behind the ear or in the scruff. Your vet can supply either under a flock medicine prescription. Use the printed dose and route from the product datasheet or as directed by your vet.
Restrain the sheep in a corner or pen with the head held still by an assistant, or catch alone using a crook and sit the sheep on its rump.
Clean excessive discharge away from the eye with a clean damp cloth, one cloth per sheep.
Apply the ointment: open the lower lid gently with thumb and forefinger, apply a 1 to 2 cm strip inside the lower lid, and release. The ointment will spread as the sheep blinks.
Repeat the ointment treatment twice daily for three to five days. Most cases show visible improvement (less squinting, clearer eye) within 48 hours of starting treatment.
No improvement after two days of ointment, or a badly ulcerated eye, means a vet visit. Do not continue treating independently.
Reducing spread
Move the flock to a field with shade and away from dust. Affected sheep feel worse in bright sunlight and dry dusty conditions.
Control face flies with an approved repellent where feasible. Flies transmit eye bacteria mechanically between sheep.
Check all eyes in the flock daily during an outbreak. Treat any new case immediately.

attrs.cue: Sheep loses sight in one eye after treatment
attrs.cause: Corneal scarring from infection that reached deep into the corneal tissue before treatment
attrs.fix: A sheep that recovers vision in the other eye and can graze normally can remain in the flock. A sheep blind in both eyes has serious welfare implications and needs an assessment of quality of life.

attrs.cue: Several sheep affected at the same time
attrs.fix: Discuss flock-wide treatment with your vet. A single injectable oxytetracycline dose across the whole flock is more practical than individual ointment applications in a large group.
